spans.text: Why this exists:
a plain chatbot answers from training data, so it guesses about your private PDFs, contracts, and wikis — often confidently and wrong. A
document Q&A bot

fixes that by retrieving the actual passages that match a question and answering only from them. Reach for it whenever a correct answer must come from a specific corpus you control, not the model's memory.
Before reading on, predict:
if a user asks a question your documents never cover, what is the most useful thing the bot can do?

blocks.title: Target behavior: what the bot should do

spans.text: Before writing any code, name the user-visible behavior. A
Document Q&A Bot
takes a natural-language question, finds the relevant passages in your documents, and returns an answer grounded in those passages — ideally with a citation to where it came from.
Start by separating the two jobs: the
retriever
finds the right text, and the model writes the answer from it. Then decide what a wrong answer looks like, so a
validator
can catch it.

items.text: Name the input (a question) and output (a grounded answer) of the bot.
Separate what the model decides (the wording) from what the application enforces (using only retrieved text).
Keep one measurable success signal: does the answer cite a passage that actually supports it?

blocks.title: Minimal working sketch
blocks.code:
from llama_index.core import VectorStoreIndex, SimpleDirectoryReader
docs = SimpleDirectoryReader("data").load_data()
index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(docs)
query_engine = index.as_query_engine()
print(query_engine.query("What does this corpus say?"))

spans.text: Treat this as the smallest runnable shape, then add tracing, validation, and tests before production.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Before you read the explanation: which one line in this sketch is the retriever, and which line is where a wrong answer could slip through untested?
predictThenReveal.answer: VectorStoreIndex.from_documents builds the retriever; query_engine.query is the boundary where model output meets the user, so it is the first thing to wrap with a grounding check and a test.

spans.text: Verify the AI-generated version before you trust it.
When an assistant hands you Q&A pipeline code like the sketch above, check these four things specific to retrieval before running it.

items.text: Does it actually load your documents? Print the chunk count — an empty or wrong directory silently indexes nothing.
Is retrieval grounding the answer? Inspect the retrieved passages, not just the final text, or the model may be answering from memory.
What happens on a no-match question? Confirm it can say "not in the documents" instead of inventing an answer.
Are chunk size and top-k set deliberately? Defaults often retrieve too little context or too much noise.

blocks.title: How a document Q&A bot breaks in practice

spans.text: The happy path looks clean in a demo. These are the failures that show up once real users and real documents arrive — and what to harden against each.
1. Confident hallucination on no-match questions
The
retriever

returns the closest passages even when none truly answer the question, and the model writes a fluent, wrong answer. Fix: gate on a similarity threshold and let the bot say "not found in the documents."
2. Chunking that splits the answer
A fact spans two chunks, so retrieval grabs only half of it. The answer is technically grounded but incomplete. Fix: tune chunk size and overlap, and inspect retrieved passages in your
trace
3. Stale index (non-obvious)

Documents change, but the index was built once and never refreshed. The bot answers from an old version with no error — the most common silent failure in production. Fix: re-index on a schedule and stamp each answer with the document version.
Watch for:
answers that sound right but cite nothing, or cite a passage that does not contain the claim. That mismatch is your first diagnostic signal.

questions.prompt: Your Document Q&A Bot returns a confident-sounding answer that isn't actually in the uploaded document. Which part of the system is most responsible for catching this failure?

options.text: The chunking strategy in the architecture slice
The validation and tracing layer, which checks whether the answer is grounded in retrieved chunks
The LLM's temperature setting in core implementation
The hardening path's rate-limiting logic

questions.explanation: Validation and tracing is specifically responsible for detecting hallucinations by verifying that the bot's answer is supported by the retrieved source chunks — not invented by the model.

questions.prompt: When designing the architecture slice for a Document Q&A Bot, what is the core tradeoff when choosing chunk size for splitting documents?

options.text: Larger chunks are cheaper to embed but may bury the relevant answer inside too much surrounding text
Smaller chunks always produce better answers because the LLM has less to read
Chunk size only matters for PDFs, not plain-text documents
Larger chunks reduce latency because fewer retrieval calls are needed

questions.explanation: Larger chunks preserve more context but risk diluting the relevant passage, while smaller chunks are more precise but may lose surrounding context the model needs — this size tradeoff is the central architecture decision.

questions.prompt: You're at the core implementation stage and need to decide how much engineering effort to invest right now. Which approach best fits a beginner building their first Document Q&A Bot?

options.text: Advanced optimization — add re-ranking, hybrid search, and caching from day one so you don't have to refactor later
Baseline — get a working retrieval-augmented pipeline end-to-end first, then layer in improvements
Production design — implement full observability and access controls before testing any queries
Skip implementation and go straight to hardening, since security matters most

questions.explanation: For a first build, a baseline implementation that completes the full loop (ingest → retrieve → answer) gives you something real to test and improve, rather than over-engineering before you understand the failure modes.

questions.prompt: In one or two sentences, explain what 'target behavior' means for a Document Q&A Bot and why defining it before writing any code matters.
questions.acceptableAnswer: Target behavior is the specific, observable thing the bot should do — for example, answer questions using only the content of the uploaded document and say 'I don't know' when the answer isn't there. Defining it first gives you a concrete success criterion so you can tell whether your implementation is actually working correctly.
questions.explanation: Defining target behavior upfront turns a vague goal ('make a Q&A bot') into a testable contract, which guides every downstream decision from architecture to validation.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the best example of a hardening-path improvement — something you add AFTER the baseline bot is already working?

options.text: Writing the prompt that tells the LLM to answer only from the provided context
Splitting documents into chunks and storing them in a vector database
Adding a fallback message when no relevant chunks are retrieved above a similarity threshold
Choosing which LLM API to call

questions.explanation: A similarity-threshold fallback is a robustness guard that protects users from low-confidence retrievals — it's a hardening concern that makes sense to add once the core pipeline is proven, not before.
